content: The following references provide detailed insights into various aspects of HIV care, cardiovascular risk, mental health, and related comorbidities: 1. Edwards-Jackson et al. (2011) compared three cardiovascular risk equations in a cohort of HIV-infected individuals in Thailand, highlighting the challenges of assessing cardiovascular risk in resource-limited settings. 2. Nery et al. (2013) evaluated the Framingham, PROCAM, and DAD equations for cardiovascular risk assessment in HIV-infected individuals, emphasizing the need for tailored risk prediction tools. 3. Hsue et al. (2008) discussed the importance of screening for coronary heart disease in HIV-infected patients, given their elevated cardiovascular risk. 4. Nolte et al. (2014) conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of coronary artery disease screening in HIV-infected men, underscoring the economic considerations in preventive care. 5. Adeyemi (2007) reviewed cardiovascular risk management strategies in HIV-infected patients, focusing on the integration of traditional and HIV-specific risk factors. 6. Willis et al. (2012) systematically reviewed the use of validated risk scores for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease, emphasizing their applicability in HIV care. 7. Friis-Moller and Worm (2007) questioned the reliability of conventional cardiovascular risk prediction tools for HIV-infected patients, advocating for HIV-specific models. 8. Knobel et al. (2007) examined global cardiovascular risk in HIV-infected patients using Framingham, SCORE, and PROCAM equations, identifying discrepancies in risk estimates. 9. Parra et al. (2010) highlighted the non-concordance between subclinical atherosclerosis and calculated Framingham risk scores in HIV-infected patients, linking this to oxidative stress and inflammation markers. 10. Pirs et al. (2014) compared multiple cardiovascular risk equations, including Framingham, SCORE, PROCAM, and DAD, in HIV-infected male patients, providing insights into their predictive accuracy. 11. Regan et al. (2016) evaluated the ACC/AHA cardiovascular disease risk prediction algorithm in HIV-infected patients, assessing its applicability in this population. 12. Skarbinski et al. (2016) explored cardiovascular disease risk prediction in the HIV Outpatient Study, contributing to the understanding of long-term cardiovascular outcomes. 13. Markowicz et al. (2014) compared the DAD and Framingham equations in a case-control study of HIV-positive patients, highlighting differences in risk stratification. 14. Begovac et al. (2015) analyzed four international cardiovascular disease prediction models and their implications for lipid-lowering therapy eligibility in HIV-infected patients on antiretroviral therapy. 15. Friis-Moller et al. (2010) developed a cardiovascular risk prediction model specific to HIV-infected patients, based on data from the DAD study. 16. Friis-Moller et al. (2016) updated the DAD study's global cardiovascular risk prediction model for HIV-positive individuals, incorporating new clinical data. 17. Serrano-Villar et al. (2014) demonstrated the superior accuracy of the DAD risk equation over Framingham and SCORE algorithms in diagnosing subclinical atherosclerosis in HIV-infected patients. 18. Wangchuk et al. (2014) assessed the performance of essential non-communicable disease interventions in primary healthcare settings in Bhutan, providing a model for integrated care. 19. Wei et al. (2013) conducted a randomized controlled trial in rural China to evaluate cardiovascular disease risk reduction strategies, emphasizing the role of community-based interventions. 20. Burkholder et al. (2012) identified underutilization of aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease among HIV-infected patients, highlighting gaps in preventive care. 21. Suchindran et al. (2014) reviewed aspirin use for primary and secondary prevention in HIV-infected and uninfected patients, discussing its potential benefits and limitations. 22. Pearce et al. (2012) compared in-hospital mortality rates from acute myocardial infarction between HIV-positive and HIV-negative individuals, shedding light on disparities in outcomes. 23. Feinstein et al. (2015) systematically reviewed the effectiveness of statin therapy in HIV-infected patients, emphasizing its role in managing dyslipidemia and reducing cardiovascular risk. 24. Tiam et al. (2012) described an innovative approach to providing integrated health services for HIV and non-communicable diseases in hard-to-reach areas of Lesotho. 25. Chamie et al. (2012) leveraged rapid community-based HIV testing campaigns to address non-communicable diseases in rural Uganda, demonstrating the feasibility of integrated screening. 26. Kotwani et al. (2014) evaluated linkage to care for hypertension following community-based screening in rural Uganda, highlighting the importance of follow-up care. 27. FHI 360 (2014) emphasized the integration of HIV and non-communicable disease care, advocating for comprehensive service delivery models. 28. O’Halloran et al. (2020) found that integrase strand transfer inhibitors were associated with a lower risk of incident cardiovascular disease in people living with HIV. 29. Eckard and McComsey (2020) discussed the relationship between weight gain and integrase inhibitors, addressing concerns about metabolic side effects. 30. Bing et al. (2001) examined the prevalence of psychiatric disorders and drug use among HIV-infected adults in the United States, highlighting the need for mental health services. 31. Ciesla and Roberts (2001) conducted a meta-analysis on the relationship between HIV infection and depressive disorders, identifying a significant association. 32. Rabkin (2008) reviewed the interplay between HIV and depression, providing an update on clinical and research developments. 33. Bigna et al. (2019) systematically reviewed the burden of depressive disorders in people living with HIV in Africa, emphasizing the need for mental health interventions. 34. Gonzalez et al. (2011) linked depression to nonadherence to HIV/AIDS treatment, underscoring the importance of addressing mental health in HIV care. 35. Brandt (2009) reviewed the mental health of people living with HIV/AIDS in Africa, identifying key challenges and opportunities for intervention. 36. Nakimuli-Mpungu et al. (2012) explored the impact of depression and alcohol use on antiretroviral therapy adherence in sub-Saharan Africa, advocating for integrated care models. 37. Berg et al. (2007) discussed behavioral aspects of HIV care, including adherence, depression, substance use, and transmission behaviors. 38. Springer et al. (2012) reviewed the impact of DSM-IV mental disorders on adherence to combination antiretroviral therapy, highlighting the need for mental health support. 39. Cook et al. (2004) found that depressive symptoms were associated with increased AIDS-related mortality among HIV-positive women, emphasizing the importance of mental health care. 40. Sin and DiMatteo (2014) demonstrated that depression treatment enhances adherence to antiretroviral therapy, supporting the integration of mental health services into HIV care. These studies collectively underscore the complex interplay between HIV, cardiovascular risk, mental health, and other comorbidities, highlighting the need for comprehensive, integrated care approaches.
